Les communautés musulmanes et juives de: Montréal’s Muslim and Jewish communities are living with the fallout of the war in Israel-Palestine. Illustration: Nia E-K
Alors que l’attaque menée par le Hamas l: The Hamas-led attack on Israel on October 7 has put the situation in the Middle East back at the centre of global concern, and a sense of insecurity is pervasive among Muslim and Jewish communities in Quebec. From Petit Maghreb to Côte-Saint-Luc, the fear of repercussions from the conflict is palpable.
Il est vendredi après-midi sur l’avenue: It is a Friday afternoon on Bernard Avenue, in the heart of Outremont. Usually, the streets are teeming with people busily making the final preparations for the weekly Sabbath ceremony, which begins at sunset.
Mais cette semaine, les rues de ce quart: But this week, the streets of this neighbourhood, known in particular for its large Jewish community, are deserted.
L’effervescence qui règne le vendredi da: The bustle that usually fills its leafy streets on Fridays, lined with handsome buildings and walked by many children from the Jewish community, has given way to an atmosphere of unease.
Les voitures familiales qu’utilisent d’o: The family cars that Jewish families normally use to get around with their children have been replaced by police patrol vehicles and Jewish community security vehicles. This week, the Sabbath will not be like any other.
Marchant discrètement vers chez elle, Is: Walking quietly toward home, Isabelle, a Jewish woman, opens up and admits she has felt a difference in how people perceive her, whether on the street or at work.
S’apprêtant elle-même à célébrer le sabb: Preparing to celebrate the Sabbath herself, she notes gravely that the mood in her neighbourhood is not what it usually is. “There’s nobody on the streets; usually there are people on the streets,” Isabelle says, distraught. “Of course we’re being careful.”
Mère de deux filles qui étudient à l’uni: The mother of two daughters who attend university and fear for their safety, Isabelle acknowledges that she asked them that very morning to stay home for the day and to hide their religious symbols in public.
« Aujourd’hui, on leur a dit de rester à: “Today, we told them to stay home and to avoid going downtown, because there are demonstrations,” she explains. “My daughters are at home, and I told them not to go out for no reason. For me, it’s worry and anxiety.”
Bien qu’elle ait constaté une augmentati: Although she has noticed an increased police presence around schools and places of worship, she is not reassured, and says she does not know when her daughters will be able to go back to class.
À quelques kilomètres de là, la ville de: A few kilometres away, the city of Côte-Saint-Luc, where a large part of Montréal’s Jewish community also lives, has not escaped the wind of worry that has begun to blow down its wide lanes lined with huge houses and resplendent lawns.
Le parc Mitchell Brownstein est désert,: Mitchell Brownstein Park is deserted, the streets are empty, and the sight of two security guards standing watch at the entrance to the Hebrew Academy speaks to the heavy atmosphere that hangs over the area.
Restée à la maison, Mélissa Perez, une f: Staying at home, Mélissa Perez, a Jewish woman, hesitantly opens the large front door of her home. She too chose to keep her children home for a few days, for fear that something might happen to them at school. She herself has not gone to the Jewish elementary school where she teaches. She says she is now “very afraid” to go there.
Cette mère de trois enfants confie prend: This mother of three says she is taking the situation “one day at a time,” given how unpredictable things are in the Middle East. And the mood at school remains very heavy.
« On se prépare tous les jours au cas où: “We prepare every day in case there’s a lockdown,” Mélissa says, distraught. “We explain to our three- and four-year-olds what to do if you’re in the bathroom: that you have to climb up on the toilet seat so nobody can see your feet... It’s scary to have to teach our kids that!”
Elle raconte même qu’on enseigne désorma: She even says that very young children are now being taught how to “be a turtle” if a threatening person enters the building.
Une fois à la maison, Mélissa et son mar: Once at home, Mélissa and her husband only briefly mention the news, so as not to worry their children further. “I just tell them to be careful, not to open the door to someone they don’t know, and not to talk to someone on the street,” she says. “Of course there’s a level of anxiety that wasn’t there before.”
Son fils de six ans, qui marche habituel: Her six-year-old son, who usually walks to school with his kippah on his head, is now driven there by his father. Worried about their safety, Mélissa also asked her children to stay home rather than go to synagogue last weekend, to celebrate what was, this time, a Sabbath like no other.
Il est 15 h 30 rue Jean-Talon Est, à que: It is 3:30 p.m. on Jean-Talon Street East, a few minutes before prayer. The streets and café terraces are packed. Here, there is no noticeable police presence. Yet the Muslim community also has its share of worries and fears about hateful acts that could be committed against it.
Avec le récent meurtre d’un enfant pales: With the recent murder of a Palestinian child in the United States and the painful memory of the 2017 attack on the Grand Mosque of Quebec City still lingering, many Muslims have changed their daily routines to protect themselves as much as possible from hate-motivated acts.
Dans son magasin de vêtements du Petit M: In her clothing store in Petit Maghreb, brightened by a wide variety of qamis and djellabas, Sarah fears her safety will deteriorate as the war unfolds. “You can see I’m Muslim, and I’m always afraid of leaving my home and being attacked because I wear the veil and the niqab,” she says. “I avoid going out too much and I try to get around by car.”
Sarah n’a heureusement pas subi d’agress: Fortunately, Sarah has not been assaulted since October 7, but with the situation in the Middle East worsening, she admits she is more vigilant, as her loved ones have advised her to be. “It can happen at any time, for example when I take the metro; I never stand too close to the edge, I stay back, because you can get pushed at any moment,” she explains. “We’re all human, but it’s like we’re something else.”
La vendeuse confie ne pas voir « beaucou: The shopkeeper says she does not see “a lot of police” in the neighbourhood, apart from City of Montréal parking officers.
Sur le point de s’engouffrer dans la sta: About to head down into the Saint-Michel metro station, Nour, who wears the hijab, says she has felt “dirty looks” directed at her since October 7. Recently, a friend of hers was even verbally assaulted by a man in the metro simply because she was carrying a Palestinian flag.
« Chaque fois que je vais au centre-vill: “Every time I go downtown, my father tells me, ‘Be careful, you never know what people might do to you, people could attack you.’”
Portant un hijab et arborant un keffieh: Wearing a hijab and a keffiyeh over her shoulders, Amel Kassem, a 26-year-old Palestinian woman born in Gaza, went to work with her eyes full of tears. The next day, she tells us over the phone that she is tired of constantly having to justify herself over the situation in the Middle East. She blames the mainstream media for the adversity the Muslim community has faced since October 7.
« Je me suis toujours sentie chez moi ic: “I’ve always felt at home here – I’m a Canadian citizen – but now, with what the mainstream media keeps spreading, I always have to justify myself, always have to explain why Palestinians aren’t terrorists, and that’s what really wears me out,” she says.
« Depuis les derniers événements, il y a: “Since the latest events, there are people I know who ask me whether I condemn this or that act, and I find it disappointing that some people refuse to hear anything other than what the mainstream media say,” she adds. She notes, however, that she has received many messages of support from Canadians and Quebecers, which “warms her heart.”
« C’est très difficile à gérer, surtout: “It’s very hard to deal with, especially having to justify myself all the time! I find it exhausting,” Amel laments. “Sometimes I lose hope, and I don’t feel like justifying myself anymore. But then I tell myself I have to do it for my people, because I’m their voice too.”
Dans un tel climat d’insécurité, ses par: In this climate of insecurity, her parents have asked her to stop wearing her keffiyeh, even though she has worn it for about ten years. She says that hateful behaviour will not make her take the garment off her shoulders.
« Parfois, il y a un sentiment de peur q: “Sometimes I feel afraid, but I don’t wear my keffiyeh to provoke anyone, I wear it in solidarity with the Palestinian people – I’ve been wearing it for about ten years and I’ll keep wearing it as long as my people are being colonized.”
Comme Sarah, Amel avoue se tenir désorma: Like Sarah, Amel admits she now stays “close to the wall” when she waits for the metro. And for good reason: shortly after the attack on the Quebec City mosque, the young woman was deliberately pushed down the metro stairs. Having already been insulted on the street several times, she says she is increasingly wary, especially when someone approaches her out of the blue.
« Des fois, je ne me retourne pas [quand: “Sometimes I don’t turn around [when someone calls out to me on the street], because I’ve already been hit with insults like, ‘You’re a pro-terrorist, you’re an antisemite.’ Since October 7, it’s happened six or seven times that I’ve been called a terrorist and told it’s a disgrace that I support terrorists.”
Amel dit pleurer « au moins une vingtain: Amel says she cries “at least twenty times a day.” She adds that she and her loved ones have lost the peace of mind they once had.

Le 19 octobre, la représentante spéciale: On October 19, Canada’s Special Representative on Combatting Islamophobia, Amira Elghawaby, said there is currently a fear of a “resurgence of Islamophobia that has troubling echoes of the past.”
Elle évoque le traumatisme causé par la: She spoke of the trauma caused by the stigmatization that Muslim communities in Canada experienced after the attacks of September 11, 2001. “Muslim communities are telling me that we cannot let the Israeli-Palestinian conflict reopen such a painful chapter,” she says. “The memory of that dark period has been revived today.”
De son côté, le Service de police de la: For its part, the Service de police de la Ville de Montréal (SPVM) says it is following events in the Middle East with “great interest” and is urging the public to be vigilant. “Although [the conflict] is geographically distant from us, we are aware of its impact on the public’s sense of safety, and particularly on the communities involved in the said conflict,” the SPVM adds.
En date du 18 octobre, le SPVM avait rec: As of October 18, the SPVM had recorded 11 hate-motivated mischief incidents against members of the Arab-Muslim community, and 25 against members of the Jewish community, since October 7.
Selon le vice-président et avocat du Cen: According to Richard Marceau, vice-president and general counsel of the Centre for Israel and Jewish Affairs (CIJA), the number of hate crimes against Jewish people is rising in Canada. CIJA fears a sharp increase in antisemitic acts, as has happened in the past when tensions flared in the Israeli-Palestinian war.
« Ce qui se passe au Proche-Orient, à mo: “What’s happening in the Middle East, in my opinion, is going to get worse before it gets better, and it could have consequences here,” Marceau says. “The fear absolutely exists within the Jewish community.”
De son côté, le responsable du développe: Meanwhile, Yasser Lahlou, community development manager for the National Council of Canadian Muslims (NCCM) in Quebec, has noted a dizzying and “dramatic” increase in the number of anti-Muslim incidents. The number of incidents of this kind reported to the NCCM has reportedly leapt by 1,300 per cent since October 7! Every day, the NCCM receives about eight calls to report incidents, compared with one a day before.
« La communauté musulmane a peur, se pos: “The Muslim community is afraid, is asking itself a lot of questions and is thinking about things that happened in the past,” Lahlou sums up. “The past absolutely carries its weight, and the wounds are still there.”
